newsitem.title: UK: Wool prices to be stifled by oversupply in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Wool prices to be stifled by oversupply in 1997.

text.p: Raw wool prices in the 1996-7 season are likely to remain on a downward trend, according to the International Wool Textile Organisation (IWTO).
A projected increase in demand will be engulfed by oversupply in the market, limiting opportunities to increase quotations, the IWTO said in a recent report.
"Preliminary indications are that following four years of decline, world wool supplies are set to rise by around four percent," the report said.
The increase will come from the carryover of 1995-6 wool into the 1996-7 season which the IWTO put at 241,000 tonnes clean, up 42 percent on the previous year.
The Australian stockpile accounts for around half of the extra availability and the contents of broker stores in Australia and Argentina will provide the bulk of the rest, the report said.
The IWTO based its demand projection largely on Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development forecasts of a 2.4 percent average economic growth rate for member countries in 1997.
Together, Japan, the U.S. and the European Union use around 35 percent of the world wool supply, with Europe taking 25 percent.
But China, the biggest wool importer with the ability to shape the market, is likely to remain something of a wild card.
Economic growth is expected to reach 9.0 percent but China's efforts to reduce reliance on wool imports saw it doubling the rate of increase of its sheep population the 1995-6 season.

China replaced Russia as the third largest producer as a result, the report said. But China is set to remain the top consumer, using more than 25 percent of global production and importing about 80 percent of its needs.

If Southern Hemisphere suppliers can continue to fill the gap in Chinese imports left by Russia, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan where stocks are said to have been largely cleared and production continues to decline, this could have a bearish effect on prices, a source at the IWTO said.

In 1995-6 the seasonal average for the Australian raw wool market indicator was 619 cents a lb, down from 788 in 1994-5 while New Zealand's was 505 cents a lb, down from 559, both calculated in local currency.
The price of wool relative to competing fibres is also expected to remain unchanged, the IWTO report said.
